causalMechanism.primaryVector: Surgical-nerve-injury sequence: the recurrent laryngeal nerve ascends in the tracheoesophageal groove and passes in intimate proximity to the thyroid gland's inferior pole before entering the larynx, where it supplies all intrinsic laryngeal muscles except the cricothyroid. Thyroidectomy performed to treat service-connected goiter therefore places the nerve at direct risk: traction, thermal spread from electrocautery, ligature entrapment, or transection produces neurapraxia or axonal loss, and the resulting loss of adductor and abductor innervation leaves the vocal fold immobile in a paramedian or intermediate position with hoarseness, breathy dysphonia, impaired cough, and — when the insult is bilateral or severe — inspiratory stridor or aphonia. Jeannon et al. (PMID 19335706), a systematic review of reported incidence after thyroid surgery, found an average temporary recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy rate of 9.8 percent and a permanent palsy rate of 2.3 percent, with rates varying by extent of surgery and case mix. Hayward et al. (PMID 22989215) reviewed recurrent laryngeal nerve injury in thyroid surgery and reported permanent palsy in 0.3 to 3 percent of cases with transient palsies in 5 to 8 percent, emphasizing identification of high-risk patients. Alkaf et al. (PMID 41047809) retrospectively assessed vocal cord palsy after thyroidectomy and reported an overall permanent vocal cord palsy incidence of approximately 2.9 percent with left and right cord involvement of 1 percent and 1.9 percent respectively, and analyzed associated risk factors. Framing under 38 CFR § 3.310: this is a § 3.310(a) proximate-causation theory. The theory is that a disability resulting from treatment of a service-connected condition is itself proximately due to that service-connected condition, so the service-connected goiter that necessitated the thyroidectomy is the legal and medical predicate for a nerve injury caused by the operation undertaken to treat it; the theory is not that the goiter mechanically paralyzed the cord, unless compressive or retrosternal goiter with documented preoperative cord palsy is separately shown. It is not a § 3.310(b) aggravation theory; aggravation would govern only where the record shows pre-existing vocal cord dysfunction (for example, from a prior thyroid or cervical spine operation, intubation trauma, or idiopathic palsy) and the claim is that the goiter-directed surgery worsened a baseline deficit, in which case the surgical increment must be separated from the natural progression of the pre-existing palsy and § 3.310(b) applies. Chronology and the individual analysis under § 3.310(a) or (b) require documentation that the goiter and its surgical indication precede the onset of dysphonia, that the surgery was actually performed for the service-connected goiter, and that the postoperative course records hoarseness or dysphonia with laryngoscopic confirmation of vocal fold immobility; where the record lacks a preoperative laryngoscopy, the examiner must address whether the palsy was pre-existing. With that evidence an examiner can state that the vocal cord paralysis is at least as likely as not caused by the thyroidectomy performed for the service-connected thyroid enlargement — a conclusion requiring documented chronology, accounted-for competing causes, and an approximate balance of evidence consistent with § 3.102. Competing causes that must be excluded or weighed include anesthetic or intubation-related cord trauma, pre-existing idiopathic or compressive palsy, superior laryngeal nerve injury (a different nerve with a different functional deficit), viral neuritis, stroke or other central causes, laryngeal malignancy, prior neck surgery or radiation, and coincidental presbylaryngis; the rates published in the cited series are population incidences and do not establish the cause in a given veteran. No individual probability is asserted here. Rating discipline under § 4.14: the same dysphonia and airway findings may not be rated simultaneously under DC 6516 and DC 6519, and where a laryngectomy or partial laryngectomy has been performed, the schedule requires residuals to be rated under DC 6516, DC 6519, or DC 6520 rather than duplicated.

Primary condition: Service-connected nontoxic thyroid enlargement (goiter) severe enough to require thyroidectomy
Primary diagnostic-code proposal: 38 CFR § 4.119, DC 7902 (thyroid enlargement, nontoxic), with Note (1) requiring symptoms due to pressure on adjacent organs such as the trachea, larynx, or esophagus to be evaluated under the appropriate diagnostic code within the appropriate body system and Note (2) permitting separate evaluation of neck disfigurement under DC 7800
Secondary condition: Vocal cord paralysis (recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy with hoarseness or aphonia) following thyroidectomy performed for service-connected thyroid enlargement
Secondary diagnostic-code proposal: 38 CFR § 4.97, DC 6516 (laryngitis, chronic): 30 percent for hoarseness with thickening or nodules of cords, polyps, submucous infiltration, or pre-malignant changes on biopsy; 10 percent for hoarseness with inflammation of cords or mucous membrane. Where the injury is complete, DC 6519 (aphonia, complete organic) pays 100 percent for constant inability to communicate by speech and 60 percent for constant inability to speak above a whisper, and its note directs that incomplete aphonia be evaluated as laryngitis, chronic (DC 6516). DC 6520 (larynx, stenosis of, including residuals of laryngeal trauma) may apply where stenosis or flow-volume-loop-confirmed upper airway obstruction follows. Qualified-human rating review required
Original nexus theory: Causation

Legal boundary: § 3.310(a) concerns proximate causation; § 3.310(b) concerns attributable worsening beyond natural progression against a qualifying baseline. The at least as likely as not standard requires individual evidence and competing causes to be weighed. Apply claim-period rating criteria and § 4.14 nonpyramiding.
